```{r setup_0602, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(gt)
library(janitor)

process_cancer_df <- function(cancer_type) {
  # Read the CSV file
  gene_mutation_counts <- read_csv(paste0("data/tcga_data/", cancer_type, ".csv"))

  # Extract gene IDs
  gene_ids <- gene_mutation_counts |> pull(Gene_ID)

  # Return gene_ids variable
  return(gene_ids)
}
```

## Determining common genes {#sec-determining_common_genes}

Now we are ready to answer this question:

**Which 20 genes most commonly have severe mutations across different cancer types??**

Remember that each data frame currently includes all of the genes which have severe mutations in at least 10% of individuals with that cancer type.

We can use the names of the different cancer types as a vector to loop through. You have been provided with these in the file `data/cancer_types.txt`.

This file just has one thing on each line, so we can use the `read_lines()` function instead of `read_csv()`.

::: {.callout-note .copycode #copy-read_list}
### Include this code

Include this code in your `TCGA_data_analysis.qmd` Quarto file.

```{r read_lines}
ctypes <- read_lines("data/cancer_types.txt")
```
:::


Now we can loop through these. For example, if we just wanted to print the name of each cancer type, we could use the following:


```{r print_cancer_types}
for (ctype in ctypes) {
  print(ctype)
}
```


::: {.callout-exercise #ex-cancer_readcsv_loop}

In your `TCGA_data_analysis.qmd` Quarto file, using the function you wrote previously, `process_cancer_df()` and a `for` loop as demonstrated above, loop through all of the data frames for different cancer types and retrieve the gene list. Store the results as a vector named `all_genes`.

::: {.callout-note #note-messages}
If R is printing too much output to the screen, you can click on the gear symbol in the corner of the R chunk and set `Show messages` to off.
![Turn messages off](images/turn_messages_off.png){#fig-turn_messages_off}
:::

:::{.callout-answer collapse="true" #ex-cancer_readcsv_loop_ans}
```{r cancer_readcsv_loop_ans, message=FALSE}
all_genes <- c()
for (ctype in ctypes) {
  current_genes <- process_cancer_df(ctype)
  all_genes <- c(all_genes, current_genes)
}
```

:::
:::

Now you have all the genes in each file listed in a vector. Genes which are found in multiple types of cancer will occur multiple times in the vector.

Let's convert our vector into a data frame:

::: {.callout-note .copycode #copy-vec_to_tib}
### Include this code

Include this code in your `TCGA_data_analysis.qmd` Quarto file.
```{r vec_to_tib}
all_genes_df <- tibble(Gene_ID = all_genes)
```
:::

The data frame function `count()` will count the number of occurrences of each value in a data frame column. Adding the argument `sort = TRUE` sorts the data frame, with the highest number first.

::: {.callout-exercise #ex-cancer_count_genes}

In your `TCGA_data_analysis.qmd` Quarto file, apply the function `count()` with the argument `sort = TRUE` to your data frame `all_genes_df`.

Take the top 20 results using the function `head()` with the argument `n=20` to take the top 20 rows of the data frame, store this in the variable `gene_counts_highest`.

View the resulting table with `gt()`.

Plot the data using `ggplot()` and `geom_col()`. It will be easier to see the gene IDs if you plot `Gene_ID` on the y axis and `n` on the x axis.

::: {.callout-answer collapse="true" #ex-cancer_count_genes_ans}
```{r count_genes_ans1}
gene_counts <- all_genes_df |>
  count(Gene_ID, sort = TRUE)

gene_counts_highest <- gene_counts |> head(20)

gt(gene_counts_highest)
```

```{r plot_genes_ans2}
ggplot(
  gene_counts_highest,
  aes(x = n, y = Gene_ID)
) +
  geom_col()
```
:::
:::

Several of these genes are very commonly mutated! For example, in 19 of our 27 cancer types, TP53 has a severe mutation in at least 10% of samples.

Now we can compare out list of genes to those from the paper, and see if the genes we found are similar to the published ones - the 299 genes identified in [the source publication](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2018.02.060).

You've been provided with the 200 driver genes identified in this paper in their **Pan cancer** data set - so mutations found in multiple types of cancer - in the file `data/cancer_driver_genes.txt`.

::: {.callout-exercise #ex-cancer_label_genes}

In your `TCGA_data_analysis.qmd` Quarto file, read the list of genes from the paper into a vector. Then, add a column, `Is_Driver`, to your `gene_counts_highest` data frame which shows if the genes are found in this list.

Plot another bar chart based on your new data frame, but add to the `aes` function to colour the bars by whether or not the gene was identified in the paper.

::: {.callout-note #note-in}
Remember that the operator `%in%` will tell us if a value is present in a vector.
:::

::: {.callout-answer collapse="true" #ex-cancer_label_genes_ans}

```{r cancer_label_genes_ans}
# Read the driver gene list
drivers <- read_lines("data/cancer_driver_genes.txt")

# Add the column to the data frame
gene_counts_drivers <- gene_counts_highest |>
  mutate(Is_Driver = Gene_ID %in% drivers)

# Plot
ggplot(
  gene_counts_drivers,
  aes(x = n, y = Gene_ID, fill=Is_Driver)
) +
  geom_col()
```
:::
:::

Look at your plot - you'll see that in many cases the genes we have identified are the same ones as in the paper! This is great - our analysis is a very simplified version of the analysis in the paper but is able to generate some similar results.

There are also some differences, we'll discuss these in the next part of the practical.


## Review {#sec-summary_0602}

[↑ top](#)

::: {.callout-note #note-summary_0602}

### Summary

* A `for` loop repeats a task a fixed number of times.
* Each cycle through a loop is called an **iteration**.
* You usually use a vector to determine the iterations of the loop.
* You can store the results of your loop by adding to a vector or data frame in each iteration.

:::
